punchline: Two dogs got exactly the same shocks, and only the one whose actions made no difference later failed to jump a low barrier to safety.
thirty_sec: In the 1960s Seligman and Maier wired dogs in pairs to the same shocks. One could stop them by pressing a panel with its nose; the other's efforts did nothing. Next day, escape meant jumping a low barrier. Most dogs with control learned it. About two-thirds of the yoked ones never did. Humans facing loud noise did the same. He called it learned helplessness, and in 2016 he and Maier added that what's really learned is control.
